title: How Batteries Store Energy
summary: How a battery keeps energy in chemicals, sends an electric current around a circuit, runs out, and can sometimes be recharged.
poll: Batteries are one of the most useful inventions in our homes.

versions.title: A Box of Power
versions.text:
What makes a toy car go? It has a battery.

A battery is a small box. It holds energy. The energy is in chemicals. You can not see them. They are shut in tight.

The box has two ends. One end has a plus sign. One end has a minus sign.

Hook both ends to a toy. Now you have a path. The path is a loop. It is a circuit. The stuff in the box starts to change. Tiny bits flow out. They run through the wire. They go back in the box. This flow is a current. It makes the toy go.

In time, the stuff gets used up. Then the box is dead.

Some kinds can fill up once more. You plug them in. That is how you recharge a phone.

A man named Volta made the first one. That was in the year 1800.

The sun shines a lot in Saudi Arabia. Big packs save its power. Then we can use it at night.

versions.title: A Box of Power
versions.text:
What makes a phone or a toy car go? It has a battery in it.

A battery is like a small box that holds energy. The energy is kept in chemicals. You can not see them. They are shut in tight.

Each one has two ends. One end has a plus sign. The other end has a minus sign.

Hook both ends to a toy, and you make a path. The path is a loop called a circuit. Then the stuff in the box starts to change. Tiny bits flow out of the minus end. They move through the wire to the plus end. This flow is called a current. It makes the toy run.

After a while, the stuff gets used up. Then the battery is dead.

Some kinds can be filled up again. You plug them in. That is how you recharge a phone.

A man named Volta made the first one in 1800. He used thin bits of metal and wet, salty cloth.

The sun shines a lot in Saudi Arabia. Huge packs save its power for the night.

versions.title: How a Battery Holds Power
versions.text:
Lots of things run on a battery. Phones, clocks, toys, and some cars all use them. But what is inside one?

A battery stores energy. It does not keep power in a jar like water. It holds the energy in chemicals. They are sealed in the case.

Each battery has two ends. One end has a plus sign. The other end has a minus sign.

Now hook both ends to a lamp. That makes a loop. The loop is called a circuit. The stuff inside starts to change. As it does, tiny bits called electrons flow out of the minus end. They move through the wire and back to the plus end. This flow is called a current. The current lights the lamp.

After a long time, the stuff inside is used up. Then the battery is dead.

Some kinds can be used again. When you plug one in, the charger pushes the stuff back the way it was. That is how you recharge a phone.

The first battery was made by Alessandro Volta in 1800. He made a stack of metal disks. Each pair had a wet, salty cloth in between.

The sun shines most days in Saudi Arabia. Big banks of batteries save its power. Then it can be used at night.

versions.title: How Batteries Store Energy
versions.text:
Phones, flashlights, toys, and even some cars run on batteries. A battery is small, but it can keep a phone working all day. How does it do that?

A battery does not hold power the way a cup holds water. It stores energy in chemicals that are sealed in its case. The energy waits there until you need it.

Each battery has two ends, called terminals. One has a plus sign, and the other has a minus sign.

Say you join both ends to a lamp with wires. Now they form a full loop called a circuit. The chemicals inside start to react. This pushes tiny bits called electrons out of the minus end. The electrons move through the wire, pass through the lamp, and go back to the plus end. This flow is called an electric current, and it makes the lamp glow.

In time, the chemicals get used up, and the battery goes dead.

Some kinds can be used again and again. When you recharge a phone, the charger pushes power back in. This turns the chemicals back to the way they were.

A man from Italy named Alessandro Volta built the first battery in 1800. He made a stack of zinc and copper disks. He put cloth soaked in salt water between them.

In Saudi Arabia, huge batteries now store power from the sun. That way, it is ready at night.

versions.title: How Batteries Store Energy
versions.text:
Phones, flashlights, and even some cars need batteries. A battery is small enough to fit in your hand, yet it can keep a phone running all day. So what goes on inside it?

A battery does not hold power the way a bottle holds water. It stores energy in chemicals that are sealed in its case. The energy stays locked up until it is used.

Each battery has two ends, called terminals. One is the plus end, and the other is the minus end. Between them is a paste or liquid called the electrolyte.

Say you join both terminals to a lamp with wires. This makes a full loop called a circuit. The chemicals inside then start a reaction. It pushes tiny bits called electrons out of the minus end. They move along the wire, pass through the lamp, and go back to the plus end. This flow of electrons is an electric current, and it makes the lamp glow. All the while, the electrolyte lets the reaction keep going inside.

When the chemicals are used up, the reaction stops. Now the battery is dead.

A rechargeable battery is not like that. When you plug in a phone, the charger pushes power back in. This turns the chemicals back to the way they were, so they can be used once more.

The first battery was built in 1800 by Alessandro Volta, a man from Italy. He stacked zinc and copper disks. Between each pair, he put cloth soaked in salt water.

Saudi Arabia is now building huge batteries that store power from the sun. That way, it is ready when the sun goes down.

versions.title: How Batteries Store Energy
versions.text:
Phones, flashlights, and even some cars need batteries. A battery may be small enough to fit in your hand, yet it can keep a phone running all day long. To see how, we have to look at what goes on inside the case.

A battery does not hold power the way a bottle holds water. Instead, it stores energy in chemicals that are sealed inside, and the energy stays locked up until the battery is joined to something.

Each battery has two ends, called terminals. The plus end is the positive terminal, and the minus end is the negative terminal. Between them is a paste or liquid called the electrolyte.

When wires join both terminals to a lamp, they form a full path called a circuit. The chemicals inside then start a reaction that pushes tiny bits called electrons out of the negative end. The electrons move along the wire, pass through the lamp, and go back to the positive end. This flow of electrons is an electric current, and it is what makes the lamp glow. All the while, the electrolyte lets the reaction keep going inside.

In the end, the chemicals are used up, the reaction stops, and the battery is dead.

A rechargeable battery works in a different way. When you plug in a phone, the charger pushes power back into the battery. This turns the chemicals back to the way they were, so they can be used again.

The first true battery was built in 1800 by Alessandro Volta, a scientist from Italy. He stacked zinc and copper disks with cloth soaked in salt water between each pair.

Today, Saudi Arabia is building huge batteries that store power from the sun, so there is still power when the sun goes down.

versions.text:
Phones, flashlights, and even some cars depend on batteries each day. Although a battery may be small enough to fit in your hand, it can keep a phone running for a whole day. To see how this is possible, we have to look closely at what goes on inside its case.

A battery does not hold power the way a bottle holds water. Instead, it stores energy in chemicals that are sealed inside, and that energy stays locked away until the battery is joined to something that needs power.

Each battery has two ends, called terminals. The positive terminal is marked with a plus sign, while the negative terminal is marked with a minus sign. Between them is a paste or liquid called the electrolyte, which keeps the two sides apart.

When wires join both terminals to a lamp, they form a full path called a circuit. The chemicals inside then start a reaction that sends tiny bits called electrons out of the negative end. The electrons move along the wire, pass through the lamp, and then go back to the positive end. This flow of electrons is an electric current, and it is what makes the lamp glow. All the while, the electrolyte lets the reaction keep going inside the battery.

In the end, the chemicals are used up, the reaction stops, and the battery is said to be dead.

A rechargeable battery works in a different way. When you plug in a phone, the charger pushes power back into the battery, which turns the chemicals back to the way they were so they can be used again and again.

The first true battery was built in 1800 by Alessandro Volta, a scientist from Italy, who stacked zinc and copper disks with cloth soaked in salt water between each pair.

Today, Saudi Arabia is building huge batteries that store power from the sun, so that there is still plenty of power long after the sun goes down.

Phones, flashlights, and a growing number of cars depend on batteries every day. Although a battery is often small enough to fit in your hand, it can keep a phone running for a whole day. To understand how this is possible, we need to look closely at what happens inside its sealed case.

Each battery has two ends, called terminals. The positive terminal is marked with a plus sign, while the negative terminal is marked with a minus sign. Between them is a paste or liquid called the electrolyte, which keeps the two sides apart but still lets certain tiny bits pass through it.

When wires join both terminals to a lamp, they form a complete path called a circuit. The chemicals inside then start a reaction that sends tiny bits called electrons out of the negative end. The electrons travel along the wire, pass through the lamp, and finally return to the positive end. This steady flow of electrons is an electric current, and it is exactly what makes the lamp glow. All the while, the electrolyte allows the reaction to keep going inside the battery.

In the end, the chemicals are used up, the reaction stops, and the battery is said to be dead.

A rechargeable battery works in a different way. When you plug in a phone, the charger forces power back into the battery, which turns the chemicals back to the way they were so they can be used many times.

The first true battery was built in 1800 by Alessandro Volta, a scientist from Italy, who stacked zinc and copper disks with cloth soaked in salt water between each pair.

Today, Saudi Arabia is building huge batteries that store power from the sun, so that there is still plenty of power long after the sun has set.

versions.title: How Batteries Store Energy
versions.text:
Phones, flashlights, and a growing number of cars depend on batteries every day. Although a battery is often small enough to fit in your hand, it can keep a phone running for a whole day, which raises a good question about what is really happening inside its sealed case.

A battery does not hold power in the way that a bottle holds water. Instead, it stores energy in chemical form, and that energy stays locked away until the battery is joined to something that needs power, when the battery starts to convert it into electricity.

Each battery has two ends, called terminals, and each terminal is joined to a material called an electrode. The positive terminal is marked with a plus sign, while the negative terminal is marked with a minus sign. Between the two electrodes is a paste or liquid called the electrolyte, which keeps them apart but still lets tiny charged bits called ions pass through it.

When wires join both terminals to a lamp, they form a complete path called a circuit, and a reaction begins that sends tiny bits called electrons out of the negative electrode. Because the electrons cannot cross the electrolyte, they travel along the wire instead, pass through the lamp, and finally reach the positive electrode. This steady flow of electrons is an electric current, and it is exactly what makes the lamp glow. At the same time, ions move through the electrolyte inside the battery, which keeps the reaction in balance.

In the end, the chemicals are used up, the reaction stops, and the battery is said to be dead.

A rechargeable battery, such as the lithium battery in a phone, works in a different way. When you plug it in, the charger forces power back into it, which reverses the reaction and resets the chemicals so they can be used many times.

The first true battery was built in 1800 by Alessandro Volta, a scientist from Italy, who stacked zinc and copper disks with cloth soaked in salt water between each pair, and the word voltage comes from his name.

Today, Saudi Arabia is building huge battery systems that store power from the sun, so that there is still plenty of power long after the sun has set.

versions.title: How Batteries Store Energy
versions.text:
Phones, flashlights, and a growing number of cars depend on batteries every day. Although a typical battery is small enough to fit in your hand, it can keep a phone running for an entire day, which raises an interesting question about what is really happening inside its sealed case.

A battery does not hold electricity in the way that a bottle holds water. Instead, it stores energy in chemical form, and that energy stays locked away until the battery is connected to something that needs power, at which point the battery begins to convert it into electricity.

Each battery has two ends, called terminals, and each terminal is attached to a material called an electrode. The positive terminal is marked with a plus sign, while the negative terminal is marked with a minus sign. Between the two electrodes is a paste or liquid called the electrolyte, which keeps them apart but still allows tiny charged particles called ions to pass through it.

When wires connect both terminals to a lamp, they form a complete path called a circuit, and a chemical reaction begins that releases tiny particles called electrons at the negative electrode. Because the electrons cannot cross the electrolyte, they travel along the wire instead, pass through the lamp, and finally reach the positive electrode. This steady flow of electrons is an electric current, and it is exactly what makes the lamp glow. At the same time, ions move through the electrolyte inside the battery, which keeps the reaction balanced.

In the end, the chemicals are used up, the reaction stops, and the battery is said to be dead.

A rechargeable battery, such as the lithium battery inside a phone, works in a different way. When it is plugged in, the charger forces electricity back into it, which reverses the reaction and restores the chemicals so they can convert their stored energy again and again.

The first true battery was built in 1800 by Alessandro Volta, an Italian scientist who stacked zinc and copper disks with cloth soaked in salt water between each pair, and the word voltage, which describes the push of a battery, comes from his name.

Today, Saudi Arabia is building enormous battery systems that store energy from the sun, so that electricity is still available long after the sun has set.

versions.title: How Batteries Store Energy
versions.text:
Smartphones, flashlights, and a growing number of electric cars depend on batteries every day. Although a typical battery is small enough to fit comfortably in your hand, it can keep a phone operating for an entire day, which raises an interesting question about what is actually happening inside its sealed case.

A battery does not store electricity in the way that a bottle stores water. Instead, it stores energy in chemical form, and that energy remains locked away until the battery is connected to a device that requires power, at which point the battery begins to convert chemical energy into electrical energy.

Every battery has two ends, called terminals, and each terminal is attached to a material called an electrode. The positive terminal is marked with a plus sign, while the negative terminal is marked with a minus sign. Between the two electrodes lies a paste or liquid called the electrolyte, which keeps them apart while still allowing tiny charged particles called ions to travel through it.

When wires connect both terminals to a lamp, they form a complete path called a circuit, and a chemical reaction begins that releases tiny particles called electrons at the negative electrode. Because the electrons cannot cross the electrolyte, they travel along the outside wire instead, pass through the lamp, and eventually reach the positive electrode. This continuous flow of electrons is an electric current, and it is precisely what makes the lamp glow. At the same time, ions move through the electrolyte inside the battery, which keeps the whole reaction balanced.

Eventually the chemicals are used up, the reaction stops, and the battery is considered dead.

A rechargeable battery, such as the lithium-ion battery inside a smartphone, works differently. When it is connected to a charger, electricity is forced back into it, which reverses the chemical reaction and restores the original materials so they can convert their stored energy again and again.

The first true battery was constructed in 1800 by Alessandro Volta, an Italian scientist who stacked zinc and copper disks separated by cloth soaked in salty water, and the word voltage, which describes the electrical push of a battery, comes from his name.

Today, Saudi Arabia is building enormous battery systems that store solar energy, ensuring that electricity remains available long after the sun has set.

versions.title: How Batteries Store Energy
versions.text:
Smartphones, flashlights, remote controls, and an increasing number of electric vehicles depend on batteries every day. Although a typical battery is small enough to fit comfortably in your palm, it can keep a device operating for hours or even days, which raises a fascinating question about what is actually occurring inside its sealed container.

A battery does not store electricity in the way that a container stores water. Instead, it preserves energy in chemical form, and that energy remains locked away until the battery is connected to a device that requires power, at which point the battery begins to convert chemical energy into electrical energy.

Every battery possesses two ends, called terminals, and each terminal is attached to a material called an electrode. The positive terminal is identified by a plus sign, while the negative terminal is identified by a minus sign. Between the two electrodes lies a paste or liquid called the electrolyte, which separates them physically while simultaneously permitting electrically charged particles called ions to travel through it.

When conducting wires connect both terminals to a lamp, they form a complete pathway called a circuit, and a chemical reaction commences that liberates tiny particles called electrons at the negative electrode. Because the electrons are unable to penetrate the electrolyte, they travel along the external wire instead, pass through the lamp, and eventually reach the positive electrode. This continuous movement of electrons constitutes an electric current, and it is precisely what causes the lamp to illuminate. Simultaneously, ions migrate through the electrolyte inside the battery, which keeps the overall reaction electrically balanced.

Eventually the reacting chemicals are exhausted, the reaction ceases, and the battery is considered depleted, or dead.

A rechargeable battery, such as the lithium-ion battery inside a smartphone, operates according to a different principle. When it is connected to a charger, electricity is forced back into it, which reverses the chemical reaction and restores the original materials so they can convert their stored energy repeatedly.

The first genuine battery was constructed in 1800 by the Italian physicist Alessandro Volta, who stacked zinc and copper disks separated by cloth saturated with salty water, and the unit of electrical pressure, the volt, which gives us the word voltage, is named in his honor.

Today, Saudi Arabia is constructing enormous battery installations that store solar energy, ensuring that electricity remains available long after the sun has set.

keyWords.definition: the power that makes things move, light up, or work
keyWords.example: A good breakfast gives me energy for the school day.

keyWords.definition: materials that can change into new materials when they mix or react
keyWords.example: The cleaner keeps strong chemicals on a high shelf.

keyWords.definition: a full loop that electricity can travel around
keyWords.example: The bell rang when we closed the circuit with the last wire.

keyWords.definition: a flow of electricity along a path
keyWords.example: The current in the cable made the fan spin.

keyWords.definition: to fill something with power again
keyWords.example: I recharge my tablet every night before bed.

questions.stem: What is this article mostly about?
options: How to build a toy car
How a battery holds energy and makes things work
Why phones break when they get wet
How the sun makes light
questions.why: The whole article explains what is inside a battery, how it powers things, and how it can run out or be recharged.

wrong.A: A toy car is only an example of something a battery can run.
wrong.C: The article does not talk about wet phones.
wrong.D: The sun is mentioned only at the end, as power that batteries can save.

questions.stem: Where does a battery keep its energy?
options: In the wire
In the plus sign
In chemicals inside it
In the toy car or the lamp it runs
questions.why: The article says the energy is kept in chemicals sealed inside the battery.

wrong.A: The wire carries the flow, but it does not store the energy.
wrong.B: The plus sign only marks one end of the battery.
wrong.D: The toy uses the energy; it does not store it.

questions.stem: What marks the two ends of a battery?
options: A plus sign and a minus sign
A red dot on one end and a blue dot on the other
The letters A and B
A star and a moon
questions.why: The article says one end has a plus sign and the other end has a minus sign.

wrong.B: The article does not talk about colored dots.
wrong.C: The ends are not marked with letters.
wrong.D: Stars and moons are not used to mark a battery.

questions.stem: Why does a toy stop working when its battery is dead?
options: The toy is too old
The wires inside the toy have melted
The plus end fell off
The chemicals inside are used up
questions.why: The article says that when the chemicals (the stuff inside) are used up, the battery is dead, so no current flows.

wrong.A: The article says the battery runs out, not that the toy gets old.
wrong.B: Nothing in the article says the wires melt.
wrong.C: The ends stay on; it is the inside that is used up.

questions.stem: In the article, what does the word circuit mean?
options: A kind of metal
A full loop that the flow can go around
The plus or minus sign on each end of a battery
The box a battery comes in
questions.why: The article calls the path made by hooking both ends to a toy a loop, and that loop is a circuit.

wrong.A: Metal is mentioned with Volta, but it is not a circuit.
wrong.C: The signs are the plus and minus marks.
wrong.D: The article does not use circuit to mean a box.

questions.stem: What would most likely happen if only ONE end of a battery were hooked to a lamp?
options: The lamp would get brighter
The battery would recharge
The lamp would not light, because there is no full loop
The battery would last forever
questions.why: The article explains that both ends must be joined to make a loop, or circuit, before the current can flow.

wrong.A: With no loop, there is no current to light the lamp at all.
wrong.B: Recharging needs a charger, not one loose end.
wrong.D: The article never says a battery can last forever.

questions.stem: Why do you think Saudi Arabia saves the sun's power in big batteries?
options: So power can be used at night when there is no sun
Because batteries are pretty
So the sun will keep on shining for longer each day
Because phones do not need power
questions.why: The article says the big batteries save the sun's power so it can be used at night.

wrong.B: The article does not talk about how batteries look.
wrong.C: Batteries cannot make the sun shine longer.
wrong.D: Phones do need power; the article says so.

questions.stem: Why does the author tell about Volta near the end?
options: To explain how to fix a dead battery
To share who made the first battery and when
To list all of the toys and phones that use batteries
To warn readers about danger
questions.why: That part tells that a man named Volta made the first battery in 1800, which adds history to the article.

wrong.A: The Volta part is not about fixing batteries.
wrong.C: Toys are listed at the start, not in the Volta part.
wrong.D: There is no warning in that part.

LOW.prompt: Explain what happens inside a battery when it makes a toy or a lamp work. Use at least two facts from the article.
checklist: I told where a battery keeps its energy.
I used at least two facts from the article.
I wrote complete sentences with capital letters and periods.
LOW.modelAnswer: Inside a battery, energy is stored in chemicals that stay locked up until they are needed. When the battery is connected in a circuit, the chemicals react and push electrons through the wire, making a current that lights the lamp. Some batteries can recharge, so the chemicals can be used again and again.

keyWords.definition: one of the two ends of a battery where wires connect
keyWords.example: Dad clipped the red cable to the positive terminal of the car battery.

keyWords.definition: a paste or liquid inside a battery that lets the reaction keep going
keyWords.example: The leaking battery left a white crust where the electrolyte dried.

keyWords.definition: a change that happens when materials act on each other
keyWords.example: Mixing baking soda and vinegar causes a fizzy reaction.

keyWords.definition: tiny parts of matter that carry electricity when they move
keyWords.example: In a metal wire, electrons can move easily from place to place.

keyWords.definition: able to be filled with power again after it runs low
keyWords.example: My camera uses a rechargeable battery instead of new ones.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of the article?
options: Batteries were invented in Italy.
A battery stores energy in chemicals and releases it as an electric current through a circuit.
Flashlights need more power than phones.
Every battery can be recharged many times.
questions.why: Most of the article explains how chemicals inside a battery react and send electrons around a circuit as a current.

wrong.A: Volta's invention is one detail, not the main idea.
wrong.C: The article never compares flashlights and phones.
wrong.D: The article says only some batteries are rechargeable.

questions.stem: According to the article, where do electrons leave the battery?

At the negative terminal
Through the electrolyte
Through the plastic case
questions.why: The reaction pushes electrons out of the negative (minus) end, and they return at the positive end.

wrong.A: The positive terminal is where the electrons come back in.
wrong.C: The electrolyte is inside; the electrons leave through the wire.
wrong.D: The case does not let electrons out.

questions.stem: What did Alessandro Volta use to build the first battery?
options: Glass jars filled with sour lemon juice and old iron nails
Iron rods and sand
Zinc and copper disks with salty cloth between them
Wires and a lamp
questions.why: The article says Volta stacked zinc and copper disks with cloth soaked in salt water between them.

wrong.A: The article does not mention lemon juice.
wrong.B: Iron and sand are not part of Volta's battery in the article.
wrong.D: Wires and a lamp are used to show a circuit, not to build Volta's battery.

questions.stem: What causes a battery to go dead?
options: The terminals switch places
The current flows too slowly
The electrolyte slowly turns into a pile of extra electrons
Its chemicals are used up, so the reaction stops
questions.why: The article says that when the chemicals are used up, the reaction stops and the battery is dead.

wrong.B: A slow current is not given as the reason.
wrong.C: The electrolyte does not turn into electrons.

questions.stem: In the article, the electrolyte "lets the reaction keep going." What does this tell you about the electrolyte?
options: It is needed for the battery to keep working
It is the plus sign printed on the battery's case
It is the wire outside the battery
It is a kind of lamp
questions.why: If the electrolyte keeps the reaction going, the battery would not keep working without it.

wrong.B: The plus sign marks the positive terminal.
wrong.C: The electrolyte is inside the battery, between the terminals.
wrong.D: The lamp is what the battery powers.

questions.stem: How is a rechargeable battery different from an ordinary one?
options: It has no terminals
A charger can push power back in and reset its chemicals
It never needs a circuit
It stores plain water inside it instead of using any chemicals
questions.why: The article says a charger pushes power back into a rechargeable battery, turning the chemicals back to how they were.

wrong.C: Every battery needs a circuit to make a current.
wrong.D: The article says batteries do not hold power like water.

questions.stem: Why does the article compare a battery to a bottle of water?
options: To show that batteries leak
To show that batteries are heavy
To show that a battery does not simply hold electricity, but stores it as chemical energy
To show that batteries need water to work
questions.why: The article says a battery does not hold power the way a bottle holds water; it stores energy in chemicals instead.

wrong.A: The comparison is not about leaking.
wrong.D: The comparison shows a difference, not that batteries need water.

questions.stem: A lamp is joined to a battery, but the wire is cut in one place. What can you infer?
options: The lamp will glow brighter
The battery will recharge itself
Electrons will flow through the electrolyte to the lamp
The lamp will not glow, because the circuit is broken
questions.why: The article explains that the electrons need a complete loop, or circuit, to travel from one terminal to the other.

wrong.A: A broken path stops the current instead of making it stronger.
wrong.B: Only a charger can recharge a battery.
wrong.C: The electrolyte is inside the battery and cannot carry electrons to the lamp.

MID.prompt: Describe the path that electrons take when a battery lights a lamp, and explain what makes the battery stop working. Use details from the article.
checklist: I described the path from one terminal to the other in order.
I explained why a battery goes dead.
I used words from the article such as circuit, current, and reaction.
MID.modelAnswer: When a battery powers a lamp, electrons flow out of the minus terminal, travel along the wire, pass through the lamp to make it glow, and then return to the plus terminal. Inside the battery, a chemical reaction keeps pushing more electrons out, with the electrolyte letting the reaction continue. A battery stops working, or goes dead, once all of its chemicals have been used up by the reaction, unless it is a rechargeable battery that can have its chemicals restored.

keyWords.definition: a material inside a battery, joined to a terminal, where the reaction gives off or takes in electrons
keyWords.example: Each electrode in the science-kit battery was a thin strip of metal.

keyWords.definition: tiny particles that carry an electric charge

keyWords.definition: a very light metal used in many modern batteries

keyWords.definition: to change something from one form into another

keyWords.definition: to make something go back the opposite way

questions.stem: Which statement best summarizes the article?

A lamp

questions.why: The article says each terminal is joined to a material called an electrode.

wrong.A: A charger is attached only when recharging.
wrong.B: A lamp is something the battery powers, not part of it.
wrong.C: The electrolyte lies between the electrodes.

questions.stem: When the article says a charger "reverses the reaction," it means the charger
options: makes the reaction run backward, restoring the original chemicals
stops the battery from ever working again after it has gone dead
turns the electrolyte into a wire
makes the battery lighter
questions.why: Reverse means to go back the opposite way; the charger pushes the chemicals back to their starting form.

wrong.B: Recharging lets the battery work again.
wrong.C: The electrolyte stays inside the battery.

questions.stem: How does the article organize its explanation of how a battery works?
options: As a list of famous inventors
As an argument for and against batteries
In sequence, from the battery's parts, to the flow of electrons, to what happens when it runs out or is recharged
As a story told by a battery
questions.why: The article describes the parts first, then the steps of the current, then the end of the reaction and recharging.

wrong.A: Only one inventor, Volta, is mentioned.
wrong.B: The article explains; it does not argue for and against.
wrong.D: The article is nonfiction, not told by a battery.

questions.stem: The ions moving inside the battery keep the reaction "balanced." What can you infer would happen if the ions could not move?
options: The battery would produce more current
The reaction would soon stop, and so would the current
The electrons would have to go through the electrolyte instead
The battery would recharge itself
questions.why: Since the moving ions keep the reaction balanced, blocking them would stop the reaction, and with it the flow of electrons.

wrong.A: Blocking a needed part would not increase the current.
wrong.C: The article says electrons cannot cross the electrolyte.

questions.stem: Why might the author end the article with Saudi Arabia's battery systems?
options: To prove that phones use too much power
To explain how Volta's battery worked
To show that batteries are only for small devices
To show that the same idea is now used on a huge scale to save solar energy for nighttime
questions.why: Ending with huge systems that store solar energy connects the science to a large, real use close to home.

wrong.A: The ending is not about phones using too much power.
wrong.B: Volta's battery is explained in the paragraph before.
wrong.C: The ending shows the opposite: batteries can be enormous.

HIGH.prompt: Explain how a rechargeable battery is different from one that is thrown away when it is dead. Use the words electrode, ions, and reverse in your answer.
checklist: I explained what happens inside a battery as it powers a device.
I explained what a charger does to the reaction.
I used at least three key words correctly.
HIGH.modelAnswer: A disposable battery and a rechargeable battery both work by letting a chemical reaction at the electrode push electrons out to power a device, but the two types differ in what happens once their chemicals are used up. In a disposable battery, the reaction cannot be undone, so once its chemicals convert completely, it is simply thrown away. A rechargeable battery, however, can have its reaction reversed: a charger pushes energy and ions back through the electrolyte, which restores the electrode's original chemicals so the battery can be used over and over again.
